scenes.tts: Inside your cells, something acts like a separate living thing. Your mitochondria keep their own DNA, apart from the DNA in your nucleus. And they multiply by pinching in two. Why would a part of you do that?
scenes.visual: NO fade from black: the film opens with THE CELL already drawn and breathing. A smooth BLUE cell outline fills the frame (11 wide x 5.8 tall, centre (0, 0.35)). Left-centre (-3.2, 0.4): the BLUE nucleus, a solid circle r 1.25 holding a slowly turning BLUE bead ring. Right-centre (2.2, 0.3): one big PINK bean (4.0 x 2.0) with a double outline, a row of YELLOW blocks along its inner edge with a spark running along it, and a small PINK ring of exactly 13 beads turning inside. Two small PINK beans (1.2 x 0.6, plain outline, a pink dot for DNA) drift near the top right. Dim specks drift left to right behind everything. No labels for the first second. On 'separate living thing' (inside the first 5 seconds) the big bean pulses once and the question 'A separate living thing?' (TEXT, 44) writes across the top; it stays for the whole scene. On 'Your mitochondria' the label 'mitochondria' (PINK, 34) writes beside the big bean. On 'their own DNA' the pink ring flares and that label TRANSFORMS into 'their own DNA' (PINK, 34). On 'in your nucleus' the blue ring flares and 'DNA in your nucleus' (BLUE, 34) writes beside the nucleus. On 'pinching in two' one small bean narrows at the waist and separates into two; each half keeps a pink dot. On 'Why would' both labels fade, the question at the top pulses, and the big bean pulses once more.
scenes.narration: Inside your cells, something acts like a separate living thing. Your mitochondria keep their own DNA, apart from the DNA in your nucleus. And they multiply by pinching in two. Why would a part of you do that?

scenes.visual: Do not cut away. The cell stays where it is at 25% opacity, still breathing. Over it: BIOCHEMISTRYPEDIA (TEAL), the title 'How Your Cells Got Mitochondria' (TITLE_FONT 54) and a GOLD rule. Title out in the last 0.4 s; the cell comes back to full opacity.

scenes.tts: The answer is a very old story. Eukaryotes are living things with cells like ours. Their oldest widely accepted fossils are more than one and a half billion years old.
scenes.caption: The answer is a very old story. Eukaryotes are living things with cells like ours. Their oldest widely accepted fossils are more than 1.5 billion years old.
scenes.visual: The cell lifts and shrinks slightly (10 x 5.2, centre (0, 0.75)) to make room. On 'very old story' the TIME SCRUBBER draws in along the bottom (a TEXT line from x -6 to 6 at y -3.0, end words 'long ago' on the left and 'today' on the right, size 28, and a TEXT knob sitting at 'today'). On 'Eukaryotes' the label 'eukaryotes: cells like ours' (TEXT, 32) writes above the cell. On 'oldest widely accepted' the knob slides left to about x -1.5 and a tick grows there with the label '>1.5 billion years' (MONO, TEXT, 32) above the bar and 'oldest widely accepted eukaryote fossils' (TEXT, 28) under it. The tag 'not to scale' (TEXT, 28) sits at the bar's right third. The cell keeps breathing; the pink ring keeps turning.
scenes.narration: The answer is a very old story. Eukaryotes are living things with cells like ours. Their oldest widely accepted fossils are more than 1.5 billion years old.

scenes.tts: Exactly when this story began is uncertain. But rewind far enough, and the cell comes apart into two strangers.
scenes.visual: On 'uncertain' a soft GOLD band spreads along the scrubber from x -5.5 to x -0.5 (it overlaps the fossil tick: no order between the fossils and the merger is claimed) and a GOLD '?' badge with 'when? uncertain' (GOLD, 28) sits on it; the fossil labels and the 'eukaryotes' label fade to leave only the tick. On 'rewind' the knob slides left into the gold band and the cell REWINDS as one continuous transformation (3 s): the two small beans merge back into the big one; the big bean straightens into a PINK rod (2.4 x 1.1) whose bead ring swells from 13 beads into a fuller ring of many smaller beads (too many to count; never the 13-bead ring in the ancient guest); the rod slides out through the blue outline to the right edge (5.2, 0.6) and dims to 35%; the blue outline pulls leftward (now 8 x 5.6, centre (-2.0, 0.7)) and grows five thin branching arms; its nucleus CIRCLE fades, but its BLUE bead ring stays, loose inside the cell, still turning. On 'two strangers' the blue cell and the dim pink rod each pulse once, far apart. Both strangers have a bead ring: each has its own DNA from the start. From here the knob stays inside the gold band, creeping, until s09.
scenes.narration: Exactly when this story began is uncertain. But rewind far enough, and the cell comes apart into two strangers.

scenes.tts: Meet the first stranger. It was most likely an archaeon, a kind of single-celled microbe. Whether it already had a nucleus is still debated.
scenes.visual: The BLUE cell with its five thin branching arms is already on screen and settled (8 x 5.6, left two thirds); its arms sway slowly and its loose BLUE bead ring turns at (-2.6, 0.6). Show, then tell: one second of just the cell before any label. On 'most likely an archaeon' the label 'most likely an archaeon' (BLUE, 34) writes above it. On 'single-celled' the outline brightens once all the way round (one cell). No 'Asgard' label. On 'a nucleus' a DASHED BLUE circle (r 1.2) draws around the loose bead ring, then un-draws, then draws again (it cannot decide), and a GOLD '?' badge pops onto its rim; on 'still debated' the label 'nucleus yet? debated' (GOLD, 30) writes beside the badge and the dashed circle settles, still dashed. The event of the scene is that circle trying to close. The dim pink rod keeps drifting at the right edge.
scenes.narration: Meet the first stranger. It was most likely an archaeon, a kind of single-celled microbe. Whether it already had a nucleus is still debated.

scenes.tts: The second stranger was a bacterium, related to today's alpha proteo bacteria. It could probably respire. That means a chain in its membrane pulled energy out of food. And it may have used oxygen to do it.
scenes.caption: The second stranger was a bacterium, related to today's alphaproteobacteria. It could probably respire. That means a chain in its membrane pulled energy out of food. And it may have used oxygen to do it.
scenes.visual: The archaeon's label shrinks to one short line above it ('archaeon', BLUE, 30); the gold nucleus label fades to leave the dashed circle and its '?'. On 'second stranger' the PINK rod brightens to full and swims in to (4.3, 0.5), turning a little as it comes; it shows a double outline and its fuller PINK bead ring turning inside. One second later the label 'a bacterium' (PINK, 34) writes above it, and on 'alpha' the line 'alphaproteobacteria relative' (TEXT, 28) under that. On 'probably respire' a row of YELLOW blocks lights along the rod's inner edge. On 'a chain' a yellow spark starts running along the row and the second line TRANSFORMS into 'a chain: energy from food' (YELLOW, 28) with 'probably' (GOLD, 28) and a small GOLD '?' beside it; small yellow sparks lift off the row. This is the first time the yellow row is named: it is THE CHAIN, and it is the same row the film opened on. On 'used oxygen' three RED dots marked 'O2' drift in from the right; one is drawn toward the yellow row and a GOLD '?' badge sits on its path ('oxygen? maybe', GOLD, 28). At most six things on screen: host, guest, two labels, the chain line, the oxygen badge.
scenes.narration: The second stranger was a bacterium, related to today's alphaproteobacteria. It could probably respire. That means a chain in its membrane pulled energy out of food. And it may have used oxygen to do it.

scenes.tts: Those are long names. Just call them the host and the guest. Somehow, the host came to enclose the guest. What do you expect will happen next?
scenes.visual: The red dots and the two gold oxygen/probably badges fade as the scene opens; 'archaeon', 'a bacterium' and 'alphaproteobacteria relative' are back as plain labels. On 'long names' every label on screen shakes once. On 'the host and the guest' ALL labels transform into two big words: 'HOST' (BLUE, 48) above the blue cell and 'GUEST' (PINK, 48) above the rod. On 'Somehow' the guest drifts left until it touches the host between two arms, and those two arms curl slowly around it (3 s) while a GOLD '?' badge with 'how? one proposed way' (GOLD, 28) sits at the wrap. On 'enclose the guest' the arms close, the outline seals, and the guest floats free INSIDE the host at (-0.6, 0.6), its yellow spark still running; the HOST and GUEST words follow their owners. The picture shows a smaller cell inside a larger one: relative size only, no scale bar, no sizes in numbers. On 'What do you expect' the gold 'how?' badge fades and the question 'What happens next?' (TEXT, 44) writes across the top.
scenes.narration: Those are long names. Just call them the host and the guest. Somehow, the host came to enclose the guest. What do you expect will happen next?

scenes.visual: hold the question. 'What happens next?' stays on screen. Nothing is revealed. The host breathes, its arms sway, the guest drifts in a slow loop inside it with its spark running, specks drift behind, and the scrubber knob creeps.

scenes.tts: You might expect a meal. But instead of being digested, the guest stayed. Two strangers now lived as one.
scenes.visual: The question fades. On 'a meal' a GREY ghost copy of the guest peels off to the lower left, crumbles into grey specks and is struck through by a grey line, tagged 'digested' in TEXT 28 with the strike across the word: the fate that did NOT happen, always grey. In the same beat the real PINK guest has not changed. On 'the guest stayed' the grey ghost is gone, the pink guest flares, and 'it stayed' (PINK, 44) writes above it. On 'lived as one' the HOST and GUEST words fade, the host's arms relax to short stubs, and the pair grows to fill the frame (11 x 5.6, centre (0, 0.6)) with the guest at (1.6, 0.5), now 3.2 x 1.5, still a rod, still with its fuller ring; the host keeps its dashed nucleus circle and gold '?'. Nothing here says the guest is an organelle yet: that takes 'over time' (s18). The scrubber knob stays in the gold band.
scenes.narration: You might expect a meal. But instead of being digested, the guest stayed. Two strangers now lived as one.

scenes.tts: Here is the claim. Your mitochondria descend from that guest. But how could anyone know, so long afterwards? If a bacterium moved in, what would it leave behind?
scenes.visual: On 'Here is the claim' the picture pushes IN on the guest: the blue outline swells past the frame edges (a blue rim stays at the frame border, so we are inside the cell) and the guest rounds into a PINK bean (4.4 x 2.3) at (-3.3, 0.6). On 'Your mitochondria' the label 'mitochondrion, today' (PINK, 34) writes above it. On 'that guest' the ancient PINK rod flickers over the bean as a bright outline for one second, then melts back (no gold badge: gold is only for what science has not settled). On 'so long afterwards' the scrubber knob runs all the way right to 'today' (the narrator has just said why) and the bean's inner details (second outline, ring, yellow row) fade, leaving a plain PINK silhouette. On 'a bacterium' a second plain PINK silhouette, rod-shaped (3.6 x 1.8), slides in at (3.6, 0.6), labelled "guest's free relative, today" (TEXT, 32). On 'leave behind' a column of four empty GREEN-outlined slots, each holding a '?', draws between them and the question 'What would it leave behind?' (TEXT, 40) writes across the top. The knob now stays at 'today' until s14.
scenes.narration: Here is the claim. Your mitochondria descend from that guest. But how could anyone know, so long afterwards? If a bacterium moved in, what would it leave behind?

scenes.visual: hold the question. 'What would it leave behind?' stays. The two plain pink silhouettes bob slowly; the '?' in the four empty slots pulse one after another, top to bottom, in a slow loop; specks drift.

scenes.tts: Here they are. Most mitochondria still have two membranes. They have their own DNA. Their ribosomes, which build proteins, are bacteria-like. And they divide by pinching in two.
scenes.visual: The question fades and 'most mitochondria' (TEXT, 30) writes at top left as the standing hedge. Each clue ACTS on both shapes at the same instant, then fills one slot GREEN. On 'two membranes': both outlines split into an outer and an inner line that glow; slot 1 fills and reads 'two membranes'. On 'own DNA': a PINK bead ring appears inside each and starts turning; slot 2 reads 'own DNA'. On 'ribosomes': a scatter of small PINK dots appears inside each, and on 'build proteins' each dot lets out a short PINK thread that drifts off (a protein being made: a thread, never a structure); slot 3 reads 'bacteria-like ribosomes'. On 'pinching in two': both shapes narrow at the waist in step and separate into two, each half keeping a ring; slot 4 reads 'divide by pinching'. Slot words are TEXT 28. The right-hand shape keeps the label "guest's free relative, today". Do not add words such as 'the same way': the four are resemblances. Nothing else is added.
scenes.narration: Here they are. Most mitochondria still have two membranes. They have their own DNA. Their ribosomes, which build proteins, are bacteria-like. And they divide by pinching in two.

scenes.tts: One more clue comes from genes. On the family tree, mitochondria from animals, plants and fungi all sit on one branch. That suggests this happened only once. Every mitochondrion today descends from that single guest.
scenes.visual: The free relatives, the slot column and one mitochondrion half slide off to the right; 'most mitochondria' fades. The tips of the tree are NOT one mitochondrion's halves. On 'from genes' the remaining PINK bean shrinks and rises to the top left (y 2.6) and five more small PINK beans arrive from the top edge, making an arc of six in three pairs; each pair takes ONE tag (TEXT, 28), left to right: 'animals', 'plants', 'fungi'. On 'the family tree' thin PINK lines grow DOWN from each bean, joining in pairs and then into one stem that meets at a single point at (0, -0.6): the tree is drawn from the tips back, and all six mitochondrial lines have met at that point. On 'one branch' the stem carries on down to (0, -2.0) and three thin TEXT-coloured branches labelled 'free bacteria' (TEXT, 28) join it BELOW the meeting point: the mitochondria are one branch among the bacteria. Tag 'gene tree (schematic)' (TEXT, 28) at the right. On 'only once' the meeting point pulses and 'suggests: once' (TEXT, 32) writes at the left. On 'single guest' the ancient PINK rod re-forms at the meeting point, with its double outline and running spark, and pulses; 'one guest' (PINK, 40) writes beside it. The scrubber knob does not move.
scenes.narration: One more clue comes from genes. On the family tree, mitochondria from animals, plants and fungi all sit on one branch. That suggests this happened only once. Every mitochondrion today descends from that single guest.

scenes.tts: So here is the idea to keep. A mitochondrion is not something your cells invented. It is a guest that stayed.
scenes.visual: On 'the idea to keep' the tree runs in reverse: the six beans slide down their own lines into the meeting point, the lines, tags and bacterial branches vanish behind them, leaving one PINK guest that grows to 4.4 x 2.2 at the centre while the BLUE host outline returns in full around it (11 x 5.6). On 'your cells invented' the blue outline brightens and then dims. On 'a guest that stayed' the pink guest brightens and the sentence 'A guest that stayed.' (TITLE_FONT, 48, TEXT with 'guest' in PINK) writes under it, inside the cell. Hold; the guest's spark keeps running and the host breathes. The scrubber knob does not move.
scenes.narration: So here is the idea to keep. A mitochondrion is not something your cells invented. It is a guest that stayed.

scenes.tts: But why did the partnership begin? Go back to the two strangers. The honest answer is that it is still debated. Here are two of the ideas.
scenes.visual: The sentence fades. On 'Go back' (and not before: the narrator announces the jump) the scrubber knob slides left into the gold band and the picture rewinds to BEFORE the enclosing: the host (8 x 5.4, centre (-1.6, 0.4)) regrows its arms and the guest slides out to rest against the host's outer surface on the right, between two arms, at (3.0, 0.4); the words 'HOST' (BLUE, 40) and 'GUEST' (PINK, 40) return above them so nobody has to remember which is which. On 'still debated' the label 'why? still debated' (GOLD, 36) writes across the top. On 'two of the ideas' two GOLD '?' badges rise from the pair to the top left and top right corners and take the words 'hydrogen?' (TEAL, 34) and 'oxygen?' (RED, 34).
scenes.narration: But why did the partnership begin? Go back to the two strangers. The honest answer is that it is still debated. Here are two of the ideas.

scenes.tts: The hydrogen hypothesis says the host lived on hydrogen. The guest gave off hydrogen as waste. So the host came to depend on the guest.
scenes.visual: 'why? still debated' shrinks to the top centre and stays. On 'hydrogen hypothesis' the 'hydrogen?' badge grows and the 'oxygen?' badge dims to 30%. On 'lived on hydrogen' an empty TEAL-outlined socket appears inside the host and pulses slowly: the host is waiting for hydrogen. On 'gave off hydrogen' small TEAL bubbles marked 'H2' leave the guest one after another and drift across to the host; each is taken in through the blue outline, drops into the socket, and the host brightens a little. On 'depend on the guest' ONE TEAL arrow settles from guest to host (no return arrow: the hypothesis specifies no trade back) with the label 'guest's waste feeds the host' (TEXT, 30) under it, and the host leans slightly toward the guest. The bubbles keep flowing.
scenes.narration: The hydrogen hypothesis says the host lived on hydrogen. The guest gave off hydrogen as waste. So the host came to depend on the guest.

scenes.tts: The second idea is about protection. Oxygen can damage cells, and this idea says it harmed the host. The guest consumed oxygen, and shielded its partner.
scenes.visual: RESET FIRST, on 'The second idea', in one animation: the teal bubbles, the teal socket, the arrow and its label fade out, the 'hydrogen?' badge dims to 30%, and the 'oxygen?' badge grows; under it the hypothesis NAME appears as a small label, 'oxygen detoxification hypothesis' (TEXT, 28): it is shown, not spoken. Only then, on 'can damage cells', RED dots marked 'O2' drift in from the right and top (the picture arrives with the word). On 'harmed the host' two reach the host's outline, which flinches (a short sharp wobble) where each one touches. On 'consumed oxygen' the following red dots bend toward the guest and vanish into it. On 'shielded' a soft BLUE halo arc forms over the host's right side behind the guest, and no more red dots reach the host. Red dots keep arriving and keep vanishing into the guest.
scenes.narration: The second idea is about protection. Oxygen can damage cells, and this idea says it harmed the host. The guest consumed oxygen, and shielded its partner.

scenes.tts: Both ideas fit some evidence, and neither is proven. One hint is real, though. A close relative of the host, grown in a lab, lives by trading hydrogen with partner microbes. So partnerships like this do exist.
scenes.visual: On 'Both ideas' the red dots thin out and both badges return to the same size, pulsing GOLD. On 'neither is proven' the top label reads 'neither is proven'. On 'A close relative' the host/guest picture dims and a schematic panel fades in: a blue cell 'lab-grown relative' and a green 'partner microbe', tagged 'schematic'. On 'trading hydrogen' H2 bubbles pass from the relative to the partner.
scenes.narration: Both ideas fit some evidence, and neither is proven. One hint is real, though. A close relative of the host, grown in a lab, lives by trading hydrogen with partner microbes. So partnerships like this do exist.

scenes.tts: Whatever began it, the guest changed. Over time it became an organelle, a working part of the cell. Many of its genes were lost. Others moved to the nucleus.
scenes.visual: On 'Whatever began it' the large gold '?' and the top label fade and the pair closes up again into the merged cell, filling the frame (11 x 5.6): the PINK guest large at the right (4.6 x 2.4, centre (2.6, 0.5)), its fuller ring now drawn as a big PINK ring of 40 countable beads turning inside it, tagged 'schematic: not a gene count' (TEXT, 28); the host's bead ring at the left (-3.4, 0.5). On 'Over time' the scrubber knob leaves the gold band and moves steadily right through the rest of the scene, and the dashed circle round the host's ring draws SOLID (r 1.3) as its gold '?' drops away. On 'an organelle' the rod rounds into a bean and its inner line folds into a few deep waves; label 'organelle' (PINK, 34). On 'were lost' 15 beads let go of the ring one after another, turn GREY, drift a short way and fade out. On 'moved to the nucleus' the label 'nucleus' (BLUE, 32) writes beside the blue circle and 12 beads leave in a stream, cross the cell to the left, and slot into the nucleus's ring, where they stay PINK among the blue beads. Exactly 13 beads are left in the guest's ring, loosely spaced. The 'schematic' tag stays on screen to the end of this scene. Labels never call the beads 'genes'.
scenes.narration: Whatever began it, the guest changed. Over time it became an organelle, a working part of the cell. Many of its genes were lost. Others moved to the nucleus.

scenes.tts: But it kept a small genome of its own. Human mitochondrial DNA encodes just thirteen proteins. All thirteen are for respiration and for making ATP, the molecule that powers your cells.
scenes.caption: But it kept a small genome of its own. Human mitochondrial DNA encodes just 13 proteins. All 13 are for respiration and for making ATP, the molecule that powers your cells.
scenes.visual: The scrubber knob arrives at 'today'. On 'a small genome' the 13 remaining beads close up into a small tight PINK ring that keeps turning. On 'thirteen proteins' each bead flashes in turn while a MONO counter beside the ring runs 1 to 13 and stops (computed, exactly 13); only as the count starts does the 'schematic' tag fade; the label becomes 'human mtDNA: 13 proteins' (PINK, 34). Labels say 'proteins', never 'genes' (the beads are not a gene count). On 'All thirteen' each bead sends a small PINK tile down to the row of YELLOW blocks on the bean's inner edge: the 13 PINK tiles slot in AMONG the YELLOW blocks, which stay (clearly more yellow blocks than pink tiles: the 13 are a minority of the chain's parts). The ring keeps its 13 beads. On 'respiration' the spark runs the whole row (the chain from s05, same place, same colour) and the label 'respiration + making ATP' (YELLOW, 30) writes under it. On 'powers your cells' the row glows and small YELLOW sparks marked 'ATP' rise from it in a steady stream and drift out of the bean into the cell.
scenes.narration: But it kept a small genome of its own. Human mitochondrial DNA encodes just 13 proteins. All 13 are for respiration and for making ATP, the molecule that powers your cells.

scenes.tts: What did the host gain? Mitochondria make most of your ATP. One influential idea, still argued over, goes further. It says the energy from many mitochondria let cells like ours afford larger genomes and more complex lives.
scenes.visual: The labels fade and the picture pulls back so the whole cell is in frame. On 'the host gain' the blue outline and nucleus brighten. On 'most of your' the stream of YELLOW 'ATP' sparks from the bean spreads through the whole cell and the outline glows faintly yellow where sparks reach it; label 'most of your ATP' (YELLOW, 32) beside the bean (the plain answer: energy). On 'One influential idea' the label fades and a GOLD '?' badge with 'one idea, still argued over' (GOLD, 32) settles at the top centre and stays to the end of the scene: everything after it is the idea, not a fact. On 'many mitochondria' the bean pinches in two, and its halves again, 1 to 2 to 4 to 8 to 16, small PINK beans spreading through the cell, each with a yellow glow and its own rising yellow sparks. On 'larger genomes' the BLUE bead ring in the nucleus adds beads and widens (the nucleus grows to r 1.6): the sparks flow toward it as it grows, so 'afford' is seen as sparks being spent. On 'more complex lives' the cell outline itself grows to the frame's safe edge and two curved BLUE inner membranes draw inside it.
scenes.narration: What did the host gain? Mitochondria make most of your ATP. One influential idea, still argued over, goes further. It says the energy from many mitochondria let cells like ours afford larger genomes and more complex lives.

scenes.tts: So look again. Why would a part of you act like a separate living thing? Because its ancestor once was one.
scenes.visual: On 'look again' the gold badge fades and the cell settles into EXACTLY the opening frame of s00: nucleus left, one big PINK bean right-centre with its 13-bead ring and yellow row, two small beans top right; the label 'their own DNA' (PINK, 34) returns in the same place. On 'Why would' the opening question 'A separate living thing?' (TEXT, 44) writes across the top, exactly where it was in s00. On 'its ancestor' the ancient PINK rod flickers over the big bean as a bright outline for one second and the question TRANSFORMS into the answer 'Its ancestor was one.' (TEXT, 44, 'ancestor' in PINK); then the rod melts back into the bean. The hook's question is answered aloud and on screen.
scenes.narration: So look again. Why would a part of you act like a separate living thing? Because its ancestor once was one.

scenes.tts: Every breath you take delivers oxygen to a chain inherited from that ancient guest. Your mitochondria began as a guest, and never left.
scenes.visual: The answer line fades. On 'Every breath' RED dots marked 'O2' stream in from the right frame edge, cross the blue outline and land one by one on the row of yellow blocks; each landing pops a YELLOW 'ATP' spark. On 'a chain' the row glows and the label 'the chain' (YELLOW, 32) points at it: the same row named in s05. On 'inherited' the label becomes 'inherited from the guest' (TEXT, 32). On 'Your mitochondria' the blue outline dims slightly so the pink beans stand out. On 'began as a guest' the ancient PINK rod flickers over the big bean once more, then melts back. On 'never left' the bean pulses once, slowly. The narration ends on 'never left'; the stream of oxygen and sparks continues to the end of the scene.
scenes.narration: Every breath you take delivers oxygen to a chain inherited from that ancient guest. Your mitochondria began as a guest, and never left.

scenes.visual: End card over the still-living cell at 20% opacity (oxygen dots still arriving, sparks still rising). LINE (TITLE_FONT 40): 'Your mitochondria descend from one bacterial guest that stayed.' Below it: biochemistrypedia.com (TEAL).
